target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would remove scheduling barriers for millions of voters
objection: A federal holiday does not automatically give paid time off at private employers, so many low-income workers in retail, restaurants, caregiving, and similar jobs may still be required to work and may not benefit from the holiday.

target: AG1’s assumption that the holiday is a good standalone solution for turnout
objection: Research and policy experience suggest an election-day holiday by itself is not a reliable way to increase turnout compared with direct voting-access reforms such as employer time off to vote, automatic voter registration, early voting, and vote-by-mail.

target: AG2’s claim that a federal holiday doesn’t solve the work-scheduling problem
objection: The criticism only shows that a holiday must be paired with time-to-vote protections; it does not show the holiday is useless, because the policy can be designed alongside guaranteed time off and still reduce barriers.

target: AG2’s objection that private employers would still make many workers work on Election Day
objection: Even if some people still work, the holiday can still help by increasing the number of poll workers and improving staffing and site availability at public election facilities, which can reduce lines and confusion.

target: AG1’s move from saying the holiday alone solves scheduling problems to saying it should be paired with other reforms
objection: This concession shows the holiday itself is not the main solution; the real fix is guaranteed time to vote or paid time off, so making Election Day a holiday becomes mostly a detour that could distract from the direct employer-access rules workers actually need.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday plus other measures still helps low-income workers
objection: Even with a broader package, national holiday status still does not automatically change private employers’ staffing decisions in retail and service jobs, so low-income workers may face the same work pressure while businesses and public operations absorb disruption and cost.

target: AG1’s claim that more poll workers and better facility availability materially improve voting access
objection: Those staffing benefits are only incremental; the real issue is whether voters can actually cast ballots through time off, accessible polling, and registration access, which holiday-driven staffing changes do not substitute for.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday would standardize access and reduce patchwork compliance
objection: Standardization does not create an enforceable right to time off from private employers, so the core distribution problem remains: low-income workers may still face the same scheduling constraints despite the holiday.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would reduce childcare and school logistics barriers
objection: A holiday may actually worsen childcare constraints for low-income working parents, because school or daycare closure can force them to find and pay for backup care or lose wages, so the holiday does not necessarily reduce the burden.

target: AG1’s argument that a national holiday changes default employer behavior enough to matter
objection: The holiday is not enforceable in the way a specific time-to-vote rule is; employers in retail and service sectors can still schedule workers, so the holiday alone does not reliably protect hourly workers.

target: AG1’s claim that Election Day being a holiday would reduce the need for workers to negotiate time off
objection: If the main benefit is that workers do not have to bargain for time, then the actual solution is an enforceable right to time off to vote, not a calendar change; without that right, workers can still be scheduled, denied leave, or required to work around workplace rules.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday creates more usable opportunity windows for voting and related logistics
objection: Those opportunity windows can be created more directly and reliably through expanded early voting, vote-by-mail, and registration access, without relying on employers to treat Election Day as time that matters for the worker.

target: AG1’s civic-culture argument that treating Election Day as a shared event boosts participation
objection: A civic-culture boost does not solve the core question of whether low-income and hourly workers can actually cast a ballot despite work constraints, so the cultural benefit is not enough to justify the policy.

target: AG1’s framing of a holiday as part of a package that still includes enforceable time-to-vote rules
objection: Once enforceable time-to-vote protections are admitted as necessary, the national holiday becomes an uncertain and potentially counterproductive add-on rather than the best policy tool.

target: AG1’s assumption that a holiday would reduce practical barriers by shifting the day’s schedule
objection: Public-holiday schedules can reduce transit options, customer-service coverage, and other support services that voters rely on, so the holiday may disrupt the infrastructure low-income voters need rather than help them.

target: AG1’s claim that election-critical services can simply be kept open on a holiday
objection: Keeping election services open does not solve the problem that low-wage workers may still not be paid time to vote; a holiday can create time availability without guaranteed paid time, and sector-by-sector staffing can still be uneven.

target: AG2’s claim that workers need not negotiate time off if the holiday is not enough
objection: A national holiday can serve as the enforcement lever for guaranteed time to vote if the law also includes a worker right to paid or guaranteed voting leave, so the holiday can directly address the private-employer scheduling problem.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday is redundant once time-to-vote protections exist
objection: The holiday reduces day-of congestion and coordination burdens in a way that time-off rules alone do not, because it shifts the whole society’s schedule and makes voting easier to plan around.

target: AG2’s claim that early voting is a better way to handle time-squeeze than a national holiday
objection: A national holiday still helps by creating one predictable shared opportunity window for families and community groups, while early voting spreads options too thin and does not remove the need to coordinate around multiple dates and logistics.

target: AG2’s assumption that broad public support and OECD precedent are irrelevant to effectiveness
objection: High bipartisan support and the fact that many OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays show that this is a workable, widely accepted approach rather than a merely symbolic one.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday meaningfully reduces scheduling barriers at the system level
objection: Even if there are scheduling benefits, the policy’s marginal effect is small for the people most constrained, and the most effective barriers are better fixed directly through longer voting windows, early voting, and vote-by-mail.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday complements time-to-vote rules
objection: If the real lift comes from enforceable paid time-to-vote and expanded access, then the holiday is only an add-on, and spending political capital on it risks being less cost-effective than directly enforcing the worker-right and access reforms.

target: AG1’s reliance on international precedent and polling to support the holiday
objection: International comparisons and polling show feasibility or popularity, not causal effectiveness; they do not prove that a federal holiday will change private-employer incentives in the U.S. labor market without specific enforceable time-to-vote rules.
